item.title: Proof Repair and (Co)algebra Equivalences
item.description: arXiv:2610.36669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maintaining formal proofs in response to breaking changes in their dependencies is a major challenge of proof engineering. Proof repair is a kind of proof automation that lessens the burden of this challenge by automatically adapting proofs in response to those changes. While proof repair is well understood through an algorithmic lens, it has, until now, been poorly understood through a theoretical lens. We address this gap by giving the first foundational treatment of proof repair, focusing in particular on type-theoretic proof repair in response to changes in datatypes. Our key insight is that the core component of a proof repair algorithm---a ``configuration''---is exactly an algebra isomorphism. We formalize and prove this insight, answering open questions from prior work. We then take this one step further and show that, by taking the dual of this representation, we obtain proof repair over coinductive types. All of our results are formalized in Agda.
item.dc:creator: E. G Plante III, Eric Paul, Cosmo Viola, G. A. Kavvos, Talia Ringer

item.title: Polymorphic First-Class Environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.36798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-class environments expose runtime environments as ordinary values and support a substitution-free, environment-based operational semantics. They also support applications such as first-class modules, dynamic composition of environment fragments, and sandboxing via local environments. Existing environment-based calculi, however, are mostly studied in a simply typed setting and stop short of System F and polymorphism. We present $F_E$, a polymorphic calculus with first-class environments that conservatively extends System F with a small-step environment semantics. $F_E$ eliminates all forms of substitution in System F. Term and type abstractions evaluate to closures, boxes run code under local environments, and box types expose the local typing assumptions of both. Manifest types, together with a two-sided type equivalence, play a dual role: they model type-level instantiation, and enable transparent type components in environments and modules. We prove type soundness, normalization, decidability, and standard properties of type equivalence, and conservativity over System F. The metatheory of $F_E$ is based on instantiation lemmas rather than substitution lemmas. This foundation supports polymorphic first-class modules with dynamic composition and sandboxing. We study $F_E$ in two forms. Our main presentation is an explicit, type-passing calculus that follows conventional System F. We also develop an implicitly-typed variant aligned with the semantics of polymorphic functional languages. All metatheory is mechanized in the Rocq theorem prover.
item.dc:creator: Jinhao Tan, Jam Kabeer Ali Khan, Bruno C. d. S. Oliveira

item.title: Abstract Lipschitz Continuity
item.description: arXiv:2610.37006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Abstract Lipschitz Continuity (ALC), an extensional property of functions, in particular of program semantics, requiring that bounded differences between properties of two inputs yield proportionally bounded differences between properties of the corresponding outputs. ALC explicitly discerns between two complementary forms of approximation: property-based (or qualitative) approximations, which retain a property of the data and are formalized by upper closure operators as in abstract interpretation, and quantitative approximations, which measure the closeness of data and are formalized by pre-metrics, a weakening of metrics that covers the distances arising in program analysis. Keeping the two forms of approximation explicit has two main benefits. First, it allows us to precisely relate ALC to established extensional properties: ALC is a sufficient condition for partial completeness in abstract interpretation, for partial abstract non-interference in language-based security and, with a null Lipschitz constant, for abstract robustness in machine learning. Second, it supports reasoning about ALC of program semantics by induction on the syntax of programs: we present a sound deductive system, parametric in the property-based approximations and in the pre-metric of interest, that reduces a proof of ALC for a program to proofs for its basic commands and to some explicit side conditions, which isolate what makes ALC compositional across sequential composition, non-deterministic choice and iteration.
item.dc:creator: Marco Campion, Isabella Mastroeni, Michele Pasqua, Caterina Urban

item.title: Preserving Separation Logic Specifications through Compilation
item.description: arXiv:2610.37244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Program specifications in separation logic describe ownership of resources and serve as logical interfaces for local reasoning. Compiler correctness, expressed as semantics preservation, does not by itself supply such an interface for compiled code, because it does not explicitly relate source and target resources and assertions. We investigate WP-preserving compilation: when a compiler translates a source program, the weakest preconditions that the program satisfies in a separation logic carry over to the compiled program. Our proof technique consists of a resource-aware simulation over interaction trees: it relates the resources required by corresponding source and target events, and tracks ownership through target operations, such as register accesses, that have no source counterpart. We apply the approach to a compiler from a structured imperative language to an assembly-like language, first for closed programs and then extended with modules and function calls. In the extended setting, each module can be verified in the source logic and compiled separately; its specifications carry over to the compiled module and are preserved when compiled modules are linked. All results are mechanized in Rocq.
item.dc:creator: Carmine Abate, Kleio Liotati, Franti\v{s}ek Farka, Sebastian Ertel

item.title: What Has Actually Been Proved? Auditable Paper-to-Lean Alignment with LeanTrail
item.description: arXiv:2610.35926v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Compiler feedback certifies that Lean accepts a declaration, not that the declaration captures the intended result: a repository can compile while a central theorem is weakened, merely auxiliary, or transitively dependent on sorry. Formalization progress should instead be measured against the source paper, in terms of its paper items: definitions, lemmas, and theorems. LeanTrail implements this view as a post-hoc, tool-agnostic audit: deterministic retrieval proposes candidate counterparts for each paper item in the Lean repository and, when available, the Blueprint; a language model judges statement-level correspondence, only among those candidates; and proof completeness comes from a deterministic transitive dependency audit never exposed to the model. Fusion assigns each item one of five coverage states, from Formalized to Missing, each backed by inspectable evidence. On consensus annotations of 98 items from three Lean projects, with three runs of each of two judge models, LeanTrail assigns the correct coverage state to 91.8% (Gemini 3.8 Flash) and 92.5% (GPT-6 Sol) of items. 96-97 of the 98 states are identical across runs, and GPT-6 Sol never reports a Partial item as Formalized. Uncovered items form a natural task queue for formalization agents, anchored to the specification rather than the compiler.
item.dc:creator: Fabricio Venturim, Leighton Estrada, Claudio Silva, Jorge Poco

item.title: safeL4: Rethinking Safe-Language-Based Single Address Space Microkernels
item.description: arXiv:2610.35999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Microkernels provide good features such as high security, safety, and flexibility, but their reliance on hardware-based isolation leads to heavy performance overhead, limiting their widespread adoption. Although constructing single-address-space microkernels based on safe language-based isolation is a promising approach to addressing the performance issue, this approach still faces challenges in maintaining the principle of minimality and enforcing capability-based, fine-grained access control over system resources. We propose safeL4, an approach to constructing microkernels based on safe languages. It guarantees minimality through low-level abstractions for unsafe operations, and implements a capability system based on the safe language's object capabilities to achieve fine-grained access control over all operations on system resources. We implement a prototype system in Rust, and our evaluation results show that the primitives provided by safeL4 are, on average, 1.9$\times$ faster than those of seL4.
item.dc:creator: Zheyuan Xu, Xiaobei Zhang, Zihan Li, Zekai Nie, Guangtao Zhu, Zhuang Lu, Qianying Zhang, Shijun Zhao, Haibo Chen, Rui Hou

item.title: AGDecode: Semantic Attribute Grammar Derivatives for Safety-Constrained Decoding of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.36105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, motivating techniques that guarantee the structural and semantic correctness of generated programs. Constrained decoding enforces correctness during generation by restricting token choices to those that admit at least one valid completion. While existing approaches can enforce syntactic constraints and selected semantic properties such as type safety, they either target specific properties or rely on operational pruning mechanisms that are difficult to generalize to data-dependent, inductive program properties. We present AGDecode, a programmable framework for semantic constrained decoding based on least-fixed-point semantics. AGDecode extends attribute grammars to partially constructed syntax trees, and reduces semantic constrained decoding to a realizability problem over such trees. The framework compiles semantic specifications into systems of relational constraints that are discharged by external verification oracles, such as SMT and CHC solvers, cleanly separating language semantics from constraint-solving machinery. We prove that our approach is sound and complete relative to an ideal verification oracle. In practice, solvers inevitably encounter uncertain queries; conservatively, our system can reject tokens for soundness or speculatively continue to generate until later queries resolve the entire generation. We mechanize the core metatheory in Rocq and evaluate the framework on semantic-constrained generation of C programs, enforcing path-sensitive safety properties including null-pointer safety, division-by-zero freedom, and initialized-variable usage. Our results demonstrate that solver-backed semantic constrained decoding can enforce rich semantic guarantees while incurring modest computational overhead at regular program boundaries.
item.dc:creator: Rajan Maghera, Asher Tempest Arya, Aren A. Babikian, Marsha Chechik, Maryam Mehri Dehnavi

item.title: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
item.description: arXiv:2610.36288v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) are increasingly applied to Reverse Engineering (RE) workflows. RE, however, differs from common LLM coding tasks as it requires models to reason about low-level program behavior. Furthermore, the deployment of tooling in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments limits the ability to use frontier-scale solutions. We examine whether a targeted LLM training approach can transfer distinct RE skills to open models via inverse basic-block execution: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. Fine-tuning \texttt{Qwen3-1.7B} and \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2\% to 85.3\% and from 63.3\% to 95.2\%, respectively. Frontier models still score highest (up to 99.2\%), but our fine-tuned \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} comes within four points at a fraction of the parameter count. We release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.
item.dc:creator: Ritika Poddar, Aidan Fennelly, Deirdre Murphy, Eric Wolos, Corre L. Steele, Michael Doyle

item.title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
item.description: arXiv:2610.36341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.
item.dc:creator: Jeff Shrager, Kent M. Pitman, Mia Golec

item.title: ProCerDCL: Query-Efficient Black-Box Probabilistic Verification of Deep Learning Compiler Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.36499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present \tool, a query-efficient framework for black-box probabilistic verification. Given a fixed, sampleable input distribution and a binary property oracle, \tool assesses the property's violation probability $p$ against a threshold $\theta$. Under independent sampling and stateless oracle behavior, acceptance asserts $p\le\theta$, rejection asserts $p>\theta+\eta$ for a user-specified separation margin, and an inconclusive verdict indicates insufficient evidence for either conclusion. The probability of each type of erroneous verdict is bounded by its specified error budget. To support this three-valued contract efficiently, \tool uses a single sequential test, eliminating the interval family required by the baseline. The test accounts for repeated sampling checks through either corrected exact binomial confidence intervals or an anytime-valid confidence sequence. We apply \tool to probabilistic local model semantic consistency, where the property oracle detects decision-level inconsistencies between reference and compiled executions under a specified perturbation distribution. Our evaluation covers 24 tasks across TorchInductor and TensorRT and examines sampling efficiency, conclusiveness, and diagnostic behavior. For sampling efficiency, we use paired one-model clean-label radius searches: the baseline requires 3.6-4.2 times as many unique samples under matched numerical parameters while providing a weaker decision contract. For model semantic consistency, checks at $\theta=10^{-3}$ yield 817 acceptances, 19 inconclusive verdicts, and 4 rejections across 840 input--backend instances from 21 tasks. Case studies of two documented compiler faults further demonstrate what these local verdicts can diagnose.
item.dc:creator: Zexin Li, Weibo Zhang, Linyi Li, Arvind Easwaran, Simin Chen

item.title: Certified Panic Mode: Repair-Invariant Error Recovery for Maximal-Munch Lexing
item.description: arXiv:2609.10600v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classical panic-mode recovery skips a failed scan forward by convention, promising progress but no repair-universal boundary guarantee for where it lands. We choose the resume position by theorem, via a committed-prefix lemma over certificates posted for parallel lexing (arXiv:2608.03473, arXiv:2608.09761): a position is a sound recovery point when every prefix repair whose scan commits through the certificate's returned evidence places a token boundary there. This quantifier is strictly stronger than its complete-repair special case, and at a sound recovery point the inclusion is strict precisely when no repair completes while some scan commits through the evidence. The evidence-returning interface pairs each answer with the interval it rests on, so a caller who knows what the scanner cannot check decides whether the boundary transfers to the intended input. The search provably terminates; the guarantee is relative to the active mode's automaton. For an automaton of n states the quantifier is decided exactly from the preserved tail by at most n + 1 representative repairs, and a shortest reaching repair has at most n - 1 symbols and a shortest counterrepair at most n, both tight. Every anchor of an m-byte input is profiled in $O(nm + n|\Sigma|)$ time. The shipped repair routines are the complete-repair case, which proves their contracts. In a deterministic corruption study of munch's procedure beside skip-one and delimiter recovery, every certified answer whose evidence survives the damage passes its landing check on every move, 40,885 of 40,885, while the 5,595 first answers resting on evidence the damage reached land 1,589 times, reported, not asserted. Of the 16,808 trials labeled beyond repair, 13,522 resume on a suffix that tokenizes whole, where both quantifiers are provably empty, and 3,286 stay undetermined, their damaged inputs not archived.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.26599v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is thus a global property, determined by interactions between components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the rest of the system exists. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along five dimensions: detecting communication errors in incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, generated hardware overhead, and annotation burden. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Ranjan Jha, Jason Zhijingcheng Yu, Umang Mathur, Prateek Saxena
